Not quite. Screen space is the area of the image displayed. This means that if your screen resolution is 500 by 500, that means your minimum is (0,0) and maximum is (500,500).

If your resolution is only 1920 by 1080, and you draw a square at 500, 500 in screen space, it will appear at 500, 500. If you do this in world space, then you'd have to draw in view space for that kind of accuracy. Usually, what most games will do for that level of accuracy is use a second camera to render the user interface in orthographic projection to avoid dealing with the complexities.

Local space is the coordinate system in relation to the object in question, not exactly the camera's view direction. For example, your right vs my right.

View space removes the negative numbers from depth. Zero starts at the position of the observer, and 1 goes all the way out to its far clipping plane. The view space coordinates are best described as 2D with depth, because you technically do not have three axes of rotation anymore.

I don't actually need to use volume textures. I just need to send information to the GPU about sections of the environment that need to be covered in a fog effect.

If the pixels keep track of their world spaces, then the GPU can just render the fog as a post-processing effect based on the Z-buffer. Or base it on a crude version of exponential height, or raymarching.

The problem would be that if we take the inefficient route and send every cube on the screen, that would leave the GPU with a large number of boxes to check against per pixel. It would mean that I'd need to do one of two things.

Run some sort of acceleration structure that would combine large sections of cubes together for their effects. It would fall apart if the player somehow finds a way to mix a bunch of uncovered and covered tiles together.

Or have the CPU combine as many blocks together into either cubes or rectangular prisms that are as large as possible... but this is NP hard in 3D space.

The other, and possibly simpler option, is to simply test against chunks. Which is what my tiled world is built of: 16x16xN chunks. If the dimensions are known, then we can just eliminate a lot of tests by simply testing the vertices twice in a broad search. First to see if it's in a chunk with fog of war. Then to see if it's in a division of the chunk. Then to perform a coarse check.

Assuming that you have a 3D world, you will actually only need a 2D Fog of War texture map. This map will be projected downwards from the Y coordinates of the world.

The result is a really misshaped looking fog of war texture that overlaps your geometry. This is good... because this is where the second phase comes into play.

The second part to the fog of war looks like a standard exponential height fog. It's just really thick. But the effect is powerful enough to obscure, while at the same time providing vague hints for what's ahead of you.

The way that the height fog works is that it grabs the world space Y coordinate of each pixel to draw its fog. This is fine and dandy, and really doesn't need any modifications.

The magic comes from using this projected fog of war texture as a stencil. And this will actually stop the fog from rendering in any visible areas. There will be some graphical errors, of course, as it's a screen space shader, not a volume. But it's more of a feature than an error for computer role-playing games.

To handle multiple floors, it's a matter of using smaller textures, limiting all relieving projected objects, and compositing it to the stencil layer.

When creating any game that utilizes tiles, whether in 3D or 2D, the first step often involves initializing a 2D or 3D array to represent everything, including graphical tiles, game logic, and the world itself if it features an "open world" design.

The issue with this approach is that a lot of the data tends to be sparse in many scenarios. When developers attempt to optimize performance, they often focus on making access faster without considering the implications of memory access or the number of elements they need to manipulate.

In one of my recent projects, aimed at creating a relatively large world using chunks, I opted not to initialize a 3D array map. Instead, I utilized a standard 1D array with sufficient indexes to only include the occupied areas of the map, while tracking the coordinates of each element.

For logical components, such as navigation grids and volumes for flying entities, I employed defined regions of rectangular prisms and reconstructed all necessary data at runtime as needed.

This method proved to be significantly faster and more memory-efficient than storing 3D arrays, especially when much of that data remains unused.

Game developer here... Multithreading and concurrent programming can be incredibly challenging. They often introduce bugs and performance issues quite easily.

You don't always see performance improvements, and you can inadvertently slow down programs. The challenges stem from architecture and the need to experiment with various approaches to find the right solution.

The primary factor that hampers multithreading performance is waiting. This can occur due to deadlocks or synchronization issues. You can't submit rendering calls from multiple sources without encountering problems, so you need to handle it from a single designated thread. You can perform pre-render tasks on other threads, but synchronization can consume time depending on the size of the scene. Additionally, data can change unpredictably if not properly protected, leading to crashes and bugs.

Another significant issue, particularly with certain hardware, is cache coherence. This occurs when data is stored in the cores' cache, but not always in the correct one.

Ultimately, the problem often lies with the programmers or the operating systems, while users tend to blame hardware manufacturers. Although this is usually the case, fixing it is quite difficult. It's akin to trying to reassemble a complex engine after disassembling it for modifications.

This complexity is why you often see games utilizing only a limited number of threads, with the core game logic likely still running on a single thread.

You are bound to have synchronization points. However, you can minimize them depending on your architecture.

Currently, my engine just uses actors, and most of the design is centered around minimizing the use of synchronization objects. These actors are merely proxies to their actual data, which is stored separately in a database. The components are simply instances of code that are updated and modify their own code and others.

The scripting language used is a lightweight scripting language and is where the magic happens. I've done some modifications, so it's heavily integrated into the engine. The main modification is that it's a thread-based virtual machine with a shared read-only global table. When objects are updated, they are updated on different operating system threads as if they are coroutines.

No synchronization primitives are exposed or used. If the actor's script detects it's leaving the instance, it yields the script, schedules the script it's entering, and reschedules with a dependency marker. The way it does this while avoiding a mutex is by sending a plain old data structure to the main thread's lockless vector.

The main thread, which acts as the scheduler, keeps track of threads and is responsible for giving threads coroutines to run. It does so without synchronization, as it is the only one allowed to monitor threads and provide data.

A state system is also implemented to give the user more control over how threads enter the script. This allows the user to make a thread entering a function that causes an actor to sleep for six seconds ignore the function until the original calling thread is done.
